newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU executive to defy call for fur ban.
newsitem.headline: EU executive to defy call for fur ban.

text.p: The European Commission is expected to defy EU environment ministers' calls for a ban on fur imports to force movement from Canada, Russia and the United States in talks on trap standards, EU officials said on Tuesday.

The Commission is instead likely to agree to give ministers the text of a draft deal it negotiated on trapping standards, challenging them to reject it formally if they don't like it, said one senior Commission official, who asked not to be named.
Meetings earlier this week gave few clues to the outcome of Wednesday's full Commission session, and most officials preferred to remain quiet on their Commissioners' positions.
But several predicted a victory for European Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan over his environment counterpart Ritt Bjerregaard.

Brittan's officials have argued against the ban, saying it risked sparking retaliatory action in the World Trade Organisation, while those working for Bjerregaard have said the Commission should follow ministers' instructions.

Those instructions, agreed on December 9, were for the Commission "to take the necessary steps as of 1 January 1997 for the introduction of an import ban to come into effect not later than 31 March 1997".

Ministers also asked the Commission to reopen talks with the three countries "with a view to reaching a more satisfactory agreement" on trap standards negotiated between the Commission, Canada and Russia.
"The environment ministers have taken a very narrow view of this issue which as environment ministers is maybe okay. The Commission cannot afford to take a view like that," the senior official said.
"It's a good deal for animal welfare. There's quite a lot to be said for the Commission to stand by that proposal," the official added.
The draft deal foresees standards for traps intended to kill or catch 18 species of wild animals, including muskrats, beavers, sable, lynx and wolves.

It would outlaw steel-jawed, leg-hold traps from four years after its entry into force but would leave unclear the phase-out period for restraining traps, which it defined as those which neither kill captured animals nor inflict any of a list of injuries ranging from bone fracture, severe internal organ damage or limb amputation.
National and international animal welfare groups have already damned the draft standards as a "cynical political solution" to threats of WTO retaliation.
